claims.text: Monte Carlo-induced chemical short-range ordering can enable accurate identification of high-entropy alloys with intrinsically low phonon thermal conductivity.
The relevant chemical short-range ordering consists particularly of HfTi and TiZr clustering and percolation-pathway formation.
HfTi and TiZr chemical short-range ordering disrupts phonon transport more effectively than a random atomic arrangement.
Chemical short-range ordering provides a more reliable screening fingerprint for thermal-insulation materials than random-alloy descriptions.
The initial HEA state has a near-random elemental distribution without pronounced chemical short-range order.
A combined DFT and Monte Carlo simulation can be used to promote and study HfTi and TiZr clustering and percolation pathways.
Sufficient concentrations of Hf, Ti, and Zr are required for significant chemical short-range order to form.
Near-equilibrium thermal or simulated annealing conditions permit the proposed ordering to develop.
HfTi and TiZr clusters and their associated percolation pathways act as phonon-scattering structural mediators.
Clustered regions and percolated pathways introduce interfaces and heterogeneities that disrupt phonon propagation.
The introduced scattering centers reduce the phonon mean free path.
Increased phonon scattering lowers thermal conductivity relative to an alloy with a random atomic distribution.
Explicit modeling of chemical short-range order will identify low-phonon-conductivity HEAs more accurately than standard prediction methods that omit such ordering.
The approach is expected to predict a directional reduction in conductivity relative to conventional calculations.
The hypothesis may not apply to kinetically limited or non-equilibrium processed alloys because they may lack sufficient atomic mobility for ordering.
Slow cooling or annealing should promote HfTi and TiZr clustering, whereas rapid quenching should suppress it.
Failure of the ordered samples to exhibit statistically significantly lower phonon thermal conductivity than composition-matched disordered samples would falsify the proposed ordering effect.
Failure of the simulation to outperform current predictive methods by a pre-established accuracy margin would falsify the claimed predictive improvement.
